author: Amphilochius of Iconium
occasion: A homily on the raising of Lazarus, prompted by the Johannine account of the four-day-dead Lazarus and aimed at showing Lazarus as the first-fruits of the resurrection.
argument: Amphilochius calls his hearers to contemplate the raising of Lazarus as the first-fruits of the resurrection. He argues that the Jewish leaders could slander every other miracle of Jesus but could not slander this one, because Lazarus was a well-known man, four days dead, and the circumstances of his burial were publicly known. He presents Jesus' questions, tears, and commands as a deliberate divine strategy to make the onlookers unambiguous heralds of the raising. The homily closes by urging the congregation to join the palm-bearing crowd in acclaiming the Lord.

outline.move: The homily opens by recalling John's Gospel account of Lazarus and contrasts the crowds' recognition of the miracle with the chief priests' reviling and envy, which led them to plot killing the risen man.
Amphilochius retells Martha's encounter with Jesus, emphasizing that Jesus' manner of questioning was a deliberate strategy so that all would follow and become witnesses of the raising.
Jesus weeps at the tomb to make public the suspicion the followers had about him, then explains that he allowed Lazarus to die so that all might know he holds authority over life and death.
Jesus commands the stone to be rolled away and calls Lazarus out with a single word; the risen man walks out still bound, and the witnesses are told to unbind him so the grave-cloths remain as proof.

_unresolved_facts.claim: aimed at showing Lazarus as the first-fruits of the resurrection
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καλὸν γὰρ τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τῆς ἀναστάσεως σκοπῆσαι... Εἶδες τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἐν Λαζάρῳ προτυπωθεῖσαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The homily presents Lazarus's raising as the 'first-fruits' (ἀπαρχή) of the resurrection, but this is presented as already accomplished/typified, not as something the homily aims to show; the occasion is contemplation of what has already been proclaimed in the Gospel reading.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He argues that the Jewish leaders could slander every other miracle of Jesus but could not slander this one
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τὴν ἀνάστασιν μόνην τοῦ Λαζάρου οὐκ ἴσχυσαν συκοφαντῆσαι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text states they could not slander the raising of Lazarus specifically, but the argument is broader: the homilist shows they slandered other miracles (the blind man, Jairus's daughter, the widow's son, the fig tree, water to wine) by claiming they were frauds or illusions, but Lazarus's raising was undeniable due to the public, putrefied circumstances.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The homily closes by urging the congregation to join the palm-bearing crowd in acclaiming the Lord
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἡμεῖς δὲ τὰ βαΐα τῶν φοινίκων βαστάζοντες εἴπωμεν· Ὡσαννὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίστοις
_unresolved_facts.fix: The homilist includes himself with the congregation ('we') as already bearing palms, not urging them to join; the closing is a performative exclamation in the first person plural, assuming shared liturgical participation rather than exhorting to it.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The homily opens by recalling John's Gospel account of Lazarus and contrasts the crowds' recognition of the miracle with the chief priests' reviling and envy, which led them to plot killing the risen man
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οἱ ὄχλοι ἐγνώρισαν καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς ἐλοιδόρησαν τὴν θαυματουργίαν εἰς βασκανίαν μεταβαλόντες... συνεβουλεύσαντο αὐτὸν ἀποκτεῖναι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opening contrasts the crowds' recognition with the chief priests' envy and plot to kill Lazarus, but the 'reviling' (ἐλοιδόρησαν) is of the miracle itself turned into envy, not separate from the plotting; the outline should note the homilist's rhetorical question 'Εἶδες βασκανίας ὑπερβολήν;' as framing device.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Amphilochius retells Martha's encounter with Jesus, emphasizing that Jesus' manner of questioning was a deliberate strategy so that all would follow and become witnesses of the raising
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἤδει τὸν τόπον, ἀλλ' ἐπραγματεύσατο τὸν τρόπον, ὅπως πάντες αὖθις ἀναγκασθέντες ἐπακολουθήσωσι τῷ Ἰησοῦ, ἵνα αὐτοψὶ δεξάμενοι τὴν ἀνάστασιν ἀναμφίβολοι κήρυκες γένωνται
_unresolved_facts.fix: The section emphasizes Jesus' questioning about where Lazarus was laid as the deliberate strategy, not 'manner of questioning' generally; and the purpose is that they become 'unambiguous heralds' (ἀναμφίβολοι κήρυκες), not merely 'witnesses.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jesus weeps at the tomb to make public the suspicion the followers had about him
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐδάκρυσε γὰρ ἐπὶ τὸν τάφον, ὅπως τῶν ἀκολουθησάντων τὴν γνώμην δημοσιεύσῃ, οἵαν ἔχουσι περὶ αὐτοῦ τὴν ὑποψίαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Jesus weeps to make public the opinion/guess (γνώμην) the followers had about him—that he loved Lazarus—so that their subsequent words 'Ἴδε πῶς ἐφίλει αὐτόν' would reveal their human thinking, not 'suspicion' (ὑποψίαν is their suspicion, but the weeping reveals their γνώμην/ opinion about his love, which then leads them to express suspicion about his power).

_unresolved_facts.claim: the witnesses are told to unbind him so the grave-cloths remain as proof
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Λύσατε αὐτὸν καὶ ἄφετε ὑπάγειν... ἐὰν ἀπιστήσωσιν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ φαρισαῖοι ὡς οὐκ ἀνέστη Λάζαρος, δείξατε τὰ νεκροτάφια· ἐμφανίσατε τὰ σουδάρια ὡς ὁ παράλυτος τὸν κράβαττον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The command to unbind is so that the grave-cloths (σουδάρια) and burial linens (νεκροτάφια) remain as proof for potential disbelievers; the outline should specify 'the grave-cloths and burial linens' not just 'grave-cloths,' and note the comparison to the paralytic's mat.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Mary... mentioned with Martha as receiving customary consolation
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: παρεμυθήσαντο κατὰ τὸ εἰωθός, ὡς ἐν περιδείπνῳ θανάτου, Μάρθαν καὶ Μαρίαν τὰς ἀδελφὰς Λαζάρου
_unresolved_facts.fix: Mary is mentioned as being consoled along with Martha, but she has no speaking role; the cast entry should note she is silent/passive in this homily, unlike in John 11 where she also meets Jesus.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Elijah... cited as one whose life was preserved
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κοῦφον μὲν ἦν μοι παρακατασχεῖν τὴν ζωὴν Λαζάρου ὡς καὶ τοῦ Ἠλία καὶ τοῦ Ἐνώχ
_unresolved_facts.fix: Elijah and Enoch are cited as ones whose lives were 'held back/retained' (παρακατασχεῖν), i.e., they did not die, not merely 'preserved'; the term is technical for translation/assumption without death.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Elisha... cited as one who struggled in raising the dead
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὔτε γὰρ ὡς Ἠλίας ἔκλαυσεν οὔτε ὡς Ἐλισσαῖος ἠπόρησε
_unresolved_facts.fix: Elisha is cited as one who 'was at a loss/hesitated' (ἠπόρησε), not 'struggled'; the contrast is that Jesus raised Lazarus with a single word without weeping like Elijah or being perplexed like Elisha (who had to stretch himself on the child twice, 2 Kings 4).

_unresolved_facts.claim: The chief priests... Referred to in the third person as revilers and plotters
_unresolved_facts.fix: The chief priests are mentioned in u01-open but not given direct speech; the voice entry is accurate but should note they are only mentioned, not quoted.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The chief priests and Pharisees... Referred to in the third person as potential disbelievers
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐὰν ἀπιστήσωσιν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ φαρισαῖοι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The chief priests and Pharisees appear in a conditional clause as hypothetical future disbelievers, not merely 'potential'; the voice is projected/anticipated, not present in the narrative.
